planting.note: Sow directly; reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings.

directions: Sow directly in cool soil; this classic English cos lettuce from the early twentieth century forms tall, upright, dark-green heads that fold in on themselves to blanch a firm, sweet heart. It is reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings in cooler climates. Long a favorite of British kitchen gardeners, it is still maintained by seed-saving groups as one of the best-flavored traditional cos varieties.

planting.note: Small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture.

directions: Sow directly in cool soil; one of the oldest documented cos lettuces, dating to eighteenth-century England and named for the city of Bath, it produces compact, upright, small-to-medium heads with sweet, buttery, self-blanching hearts. Its small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture, and it was historically valued for delivering a fine cos lettuce in a smaller garden footprint than larger romaines. Heirloom seed savers maintain it as a variety predating most commercial romaine breeding.

planting.note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden as temperatures drop.

directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden and firm up as temperatures drop, with a light frost sweetening the flavor. Named for the lagoon town of Chioggia near Venice, this classic Italian radicchio forms tight, round, cabbage-like heads of deep wine-red leaves once cool autumn nights trigger the pigment. It is one of the most widely grown radicchio types in Italy and forms the template most people picture when they hear the word radicchio.

planting.note: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop.

directions: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop, since it is also reasonably slow to bolt. This French heirloom butterhead, whose name translates to brown of winter, forms compact rosettes of bronze-tinged green leaves and ranks among the most cold-hardy lettuces in cultivation, often overwintering under row cover or in a cold frame. Its history traces to at least the nineteenth century in France, where it kept kitchen gardens supplied with greens through the cold months.

planting.note: Sow directly in early spring; can be harvested leaf by leaf or cut whole, often regrowing a second flush in cool conditions.

directions: Sow directly in early spring; a Polish heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, named for Kraków, with deeply notched, savoyed red-bronze leaves and a fast cut-and-come-again habit. It matures quickly from an early spring sowing and can be harvested leaf by leaf or cut whole, often regrowing a second flush in cool conditions. Central European seed keepers have maintained it for generations as a colorful, reliable early salad green.
